title: What is known about 1RB1RE_1RC0LD_1LB---_1RA1LD_1RA0RF_1RE0LC
description: Proof status of the six-state BB(6) holdout 1RB1RE_1RC0LD_1LB---_1RA1LD_1RA0RF_1RE0LC.
intro: Nobody knows whether this six-state, two-symbol Turing machine halts when started on a blank tape: it is one of the holdouts left open by the bbchallenge project. This page lists what has been established about it, sorted by what each result rests on.
verdict: The question is open. Read two cells at a time (0 = 01, 1 = 11, a = 10, b = 00) the machine is, after its start-up, a rewriting system with twelve rules on bits: D walks left to the next 0 and sets it, E walks right raising every symbol (a → 0 → 1) until a 1 or a b sends it back. It halts exactly when E reads b 0. Every macro move and both sweeps through the block are Lean theorems.

An exact accelerated simulation (trusted) ran 3·10<sup>7</sup> rounds, 8,388,105,420,665,431 steps, without a halt. The work in the irregular region is local (a round reads at most 2,731 pairs of it; the count has a geometric tail), and the step that must precede a halt has not occurred once in 3.2·10<sup>9</sup> opportunities after round 7. That points to an invariant that excludes the halt; it is not a local (n-gram) one and has not been found.

claims.title: The halting configurations
claims.text: The machine stops exactly when it reads the symbol of a halting transition (C1); the generated statement covers every configuration.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10,000 steps
claims.text: The list simulator of the shared library, proved to agree with the machine's semantics, runs 10,000 steps from blank tape without a halt, evaluated by Lean's kernel.

claims.title: The two sweeps through the block
claims.text: For every n and every tape: L (01011111)<sup>n+3</sup> 1 1 B> 0 reaches L D> (11101000)<sup>n+3</sup> 1 1 0 1 in 38n+118 steps, and L 010111 B> (11101000)<sup>n+1</sup> R reaches L (11010111)<sup>n+1</sup> 010111 B> R, 26 steps a word.

claims.title: The pair machine
claims.text: With 0 = 01, 1 = 11, a = 10, b = 00: each of the 41 macro moves (a state entering a pair from the left or from the right, and how it leaves) holds for every tape around the pair.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>7</sup> steps
claims.text: The same run, evaluated by compiled code.

claims.title: The pair machine is the machine
claims.text: Run from the end of each round to the next, the pair machine gives the same tape and the same number of steps as the plain machine (398 rounds, 3·10<sup>6</sup> steps).

claims.title: After round 387 only twelve moves
claims.text: In 3·107 rounds the last macro move outside the D/E/B system (1<D, 0<D, E> on 0, 1, a, b, 1<B, 0<B, B> on 1, a, b) is in round 387. In that system the only halt is B> 0, reached only by E reading b 0.

claims.title: No halt in 3·10<sup>7</sup> rounds
claims.text: The pair simulator with the two block rules as jumps (same step counts as without them) runs 30,000,000 rounds = 8,388,105,420,665,431 steps without a halt; the block then has 8,734,830 words and the region 25,061,030 pairs.

claims.title: No halt in the first 4.21·10<sup>8</sup> steps (accelerated run, blocks of 6)
claims.text: The run-length simulator tools/c/rleaccel.cpp (blocks of 6 cells, runs of a block crossed in one step, and cycle jumps, each used only after its one-cycle rule has been proved symbolically for all lengths above the minimums it needs; tested cell for cell against direct runs) runs 77,000,000 macro steps from blank tape without a halt, in 10 seconds. That is more than 4.21·108 machine steps. It found no rule that repeats forever, so it does not decide the machine.

claims.title: The work in the region is local
claims.text: The number of pairs of the region read in a round has a geometric tail (most rounds 8 to 64 pairs, 5,389 of 3·10<sup>7</sup> rounds more than 1,024, the deepest 2,731), while the region grows by 0.835 pairs a round: its left half is never read again.

claims.title: It very probably never halts
claims.text: A halt needs E to read a 1 followed by 0 or b with a 0 behind it. With a 1 behind it this happened 3.2·10<sup>9</sup> times in 3·10<sup>7</sup> rounds, with a 0 behind it never after round 7; and E> b was followed by 1, a or b 2·10<sup>9</sup> times and by 0 never.

claims.title: The invariant
claims.text: The constraint on the words right of the head that excludes the halt is not known. N-gram closed sets on the pair machine (up to 9 pairs a side) and finite-automaton closures with last-n-pairs automata (n ≤ 5) do not exclude it.

explainer.lede: Nobody knows, but probably not. Started on a blank tape, this Turing machine has been followed for 8.4·10<sup>15</sup> steps (by an exact shortcut simulation) without stopping. Read two cells at a time it turns into a small rewriting game on bits, and the one position that would stop it has never come close to appearing.

facts.text: No halt in the run-length accelerator (proved cycle jumps, blocks of 6).
The machine on pairs of cells, after its start-up: every move is a Lean theorem.
3·10<sup>7</sup> rounds without a halt (exact accelerated simulation).
Times the step that must precede a halt occurred after round 7.

sections.heading: Two cells at a time
html: Cell by cell the tape of this machine looks like noise next to a tidy block. Read it two cells at a time and it becomes much simpler. Call the four possible pairs 0 = 01, 1 = 11, a = 10 and b = 00 (two blank cells are a b). Whenever the head enters a pair it leaves it again within three steps, so the machine can be described by what it does to whole pairs. After a short start-up it only ever uses twelve such moves:

D walks left:    1 <D  →  <D 1        0 <D  →  1 E>
E walks right:   E> a  →  0 E>        E> 0  →  1 E>
                 1 E> 1  →  <D a a    0 E> 1  →  <D 1 b
                 E> b 1  →  <D 1 0    E> b b  →  <D 1 0    E> b a  →  <D 1 b
                 E> b 0  →  HALT

In words: D walks left over 1s until it finds a 0, turns it into a 1 and hands over to E. E walks right and raises every symbol it passes (a becomes 0, 0 becomes 1) until it meets a 1 or a b, which sends D back to the left, leaving a little mark (a a, 1 b or 1 0) that depends on the bit E had just written. Left of the head there are only the bits 0 and 1; the marks a and b exist only to the right of it. The machine stops in exactly one situation: E meets a b that is followed by a 0.

sections.heading: A zig-zag over a block, and a growing record
html: The tape has two parts: an irregular word of bits (the region) and, right of it, a block of copies of 0011. In each round D sweeps left through the block turning every 0011 into 1aab (38 steps a word), the head does some work at the right end of the region, and then it sweeps back to the right restoring the block (26 steps a word) and adds two pairs at the end. Both sweeps are proved in Lean for blocks of every length. Per round the block gains 0.29 words on average and the region 0.83 pairs.

The work in the region is where the twelve rules really compute, and its result looks random. But it is local: in thirty million rounds the head never went more than 2,731 pairs into the region, and deep visits are exponentially rare. What is further left is a frozen record of the past.

sections.heading: A stop that never comes close
html: To read b 0, E must first have read a 1 followed by a 0 or a b while the bit just behind it was a 0. In thirty million rounds E read a 1 followed by 0 or b more than three billion times, and the bit behind it was a 1 every single time (after the first seven rounds). If the dangerous case came up by chance it would have appeared long ago.

So the configurations this machine reaches obey some rule that keeps the halting pattern out. Nobody has found that rule yet: it is not a rule about short windows of the tape (searches with windows of up to 18 cells on each side fail). Finding it would turn this page's answer from “very probably never” into a proof.

sections.heading: Proved, computed, guessed
html: Proved in Lean (kernel): every pair move, for every tape, and the two sweeps through the block. Computed (trusted programs, cross-checked): that the pair description agrees with the real machine round by round; the thirty million rounds without a halt; the statistics. Guessed: that it never halts.

summary: Read two cells at a time, the machine is a 12-rule rewriting system on bits (D moves left looking for a 0, E moves right raising symbols) driven by a zig-zag over a block of words (both sweeps proved); it halts iff E reads the pair word b0; no halt in 3·10^7 rounds (8.4·10^15 steps), and the precursor of the halt never occurs in 3.2·10^9 opportunities, so an invariant is expected but not found. Accelerated run: no halt in 4.21e8 steps.
family: pair rewriting system (D/E/B on bits) behind a zig-zag block
